title: Linking words for writing
desc: Connectors from A2 to C1: how to use them, punctuate them and place them in a sentence.
intro: Connectors make your writing clear and organized. In each set you learn the connectors, how they are punctuated and where they go in the sentence. Then you practice with gaps, choices, corrections and word order. Watch for the classic mistakes: 'despite of', 'although ... but', 'in the other hand'.

sets.title: Basic connectors: and, but, or, so, because
sets.intro: Small words join ideas. Use 'and' to add, 'but' to contrast, 'or' for a choice, 'so' for a result and 'because' for a reason. Put a comma before 'but' and 'so' when they join two full sentences.

learn.def: adds an idea; no comma with two short items, e.g. tea and coffee
learn.example: I have a brother and a sister.

learn.def: shows a contrast; use a comma before it when it joins two sentences
learn.example: I like pizza, but I don't like cheese.

learn.def: shows a choice between things
learn.example: Do you want tea or coffee?

learn.def: gives a result; comma before it, and it comes in the middle of the sentence
learn.example: I was tired, so I went to bed.

learn.def: gives a reason; it comes before the reason (subject + verb), usually with no comma
learn.example: I stayed home because I was sick.

learn.def: joins two things of the same type; always use 'and', never 'or'
learn.example: I like both tea and coffee.

learn.def: shows a choice between two things; always use 'or'
learn.example: You can either walk or take the bus.

learn.def: gives a result; starts a new sentence
learn.example: It was raining. That's why we stayed home.

sets.title: Sequencing a story
sets.intro: These words show the order of events: what happened first, next and last. At the start of a sentence, put a comma after them (First, ... Then, ...).

learn.def: starts a list of events; at the start of a sentence, a comma follows
learn.example: First, I wake up.

learn.def: a longer way to start; comma after it
learn.example: First of all, we need some eggs.

learn.def: shows the next event; no comma needed in the middle of a sentence
learn.example: I had breakfast and then I went to work.

learn.def: shows the next step; comma after it at the start
learn.example: Next, put the bread in the pan.

learn.def: starts a new sentence; comma after it
learn.example: After that, we went home.

learn.def: shows a time after; can start or end the sentence
learn.example: Later, I called my mother.

learn.def: two things happen at the same time; comma after it
learn.example: I cooked. Meanwhile, my brother cleaned.

learn.def: shows the last event; comma after it at the start
learn.example: Finally, we arrived at the hotel.

learn.def: after a long wait; comma after it
learn.example: At last, the bus came.

learn.def: the final result of a story; not 'at the end'
learn.example: In the end, we stayed home.

sets.title: Time connectors: when, while, before, after, until
sets.intro: Time words tell us when or in what order things happen. Put them at the start of the sentence with a comma after the time part (When I get home, I cook), or in the middle with no comma (I cook when I get home). After them, use the present simple for the future, not 'will'.

learn.def: earlier than another action
learn.example: Wash your hands before you eat.

learn.def: later than another action

learn.def: up to the moment something happens
learn.example: Wait here until I come back.

learn.def: immediately when something happens
learn.example: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.

learn.def: every time something happens
learn.example: Whenever it rains, I stay at home.

learn.def: on each occasion that something happens
learn.example: Every time I see him, I say hello.

learn.def: after something has happened
learn.example: Once I finish, I will call you.

sets.title: Agreeing and adding: also, too, as well, either
sets.intro: Use 'also', 'too' and 'as well' to add a positive idea, and 'either' to add a negative idea. 'Also' goes before the main verb (or after 'be'); 'too', 'as well' and 'either' go at the end. To agree, say 'Me too' or 'So do I' for positive ideas, and 'Me neither' or 'Neither do I' for negative ones.

learn.def: adds an idea; goes before the main verb or after 'be'
learn.example: She also plays the piano.

learn.def: adds an idea; goes at the end of the sentence
learn.example: I like tea, and I like coffee too.

learn.def: adds an idea; goes at the end, like 'too'
learn.example: He speaks French as well.

learn.def: adds a negative idea; goes at the end of a negative sentence
learn.example: I don't like fish, and she doesn't like it either.

learn.def: a short answer to agree with a positive sentence
learn.example: A: I'm tired. B: Me too.

learn.def: a short answer to agree with a negative sentence
learn.example: A: I don't like rain. B: Me neither.

learn.en: so do I / so am I
learn.def: agrees with a positive sentence; 'so' + auxiliary + subject
learn.example: A: I love music. B: So do I.

learn.en: neither do I / neither can I
learn.def: agrees with a negative sentence; 'neither' + auxiliary + subject
learn.example: A: I can't swim. B: Neither can I.

watch.wrong: I don't like onions too.
watch.right: I don't like onions either.
watch.why: In negative sentences use 'either', not 'too'.

watch.wrong: I like also pizza.
watch.right: I also like pizza.
watch.why: 'Also' goes before the main verb (after 'be'), not after it.

watch.wrong: A: I can't dance. B: So can I.
watch.right: A: I can't dance. B: Neither can I.
watch.why: Agree with a negative sentence using 'neither', not 'so'.

sets.title: Contrast: although, however, but, even though
sets.intro: These words connect two different or surprising ideas. 'Although', 'even though' and 'though' are followed by a clause and use only ONE connector in the sentence. 'However' starts a new sentence with a comma after it.

learn.def: contrast; subject + verb follows; never use 'but' in the same sentence
learn.example: Although it was late, we kept working.

learn.def: stronger than 'although'; followed by a full clause
learn.example: Even though he was tired, he went running.

learn.def: like 'although'; can also end a sentence in speech
learn.example: Though it was cold, we went out.

learn.def: contrast; starts a new sentence, then a comma
learn.example: It was cold. However, we went swimming.

learn.def: contrast; comma before it when it joins two sentences
learn.example: She is rich, but she isn't happy.

learn.def: a formal 'but' for a surprising contrast; comma before it
learn.example: He studied hard, yet he failed.

learn.def: contrast at the start of a sentence; comma after it
learn.example: It was risky. Still, we tried.

learn.def: compares two different things; comma after it
learn.example: Cities are noisy. In contrast, villages are quiet.

learn.def: compares two things; comma between the parts
learn.example: While I like tea, my wife likes coffee.

sets.title: Reason and result
sets.intro: Some words give a reason (because, since, as) and some give a result (so, therefore, as a result). Be careful: 'because of' is followed by a noun, but 'because' is followed by a clause.

learn.def: reason; followed by subject + verb
learn.example: We stayed home because it was raining.

learn.def: reason; followed by a noun or pronoun, NOT a clause
learn.example: We stayed home because of the rain.

learn.def: reason that is already known; often at the start, with a comma
learn.example: Since it was late, we went home.

learn.def: reason; often at the start, with a comma
learn.example: As I was tired, I went to bed.

learn.def: result; comma before it
learn.example: It was late, so we went home.

learn.def: result; starts a new sentence, comma after it
learn.example: It rained. As a result, the game was cancelled.

learn.def: result; formal; comma after it
learn.example: He was ill. Therefore, he stayed in bed.

learn.def: purpose; followed by a clause with can/could/will/would
learn.example: I took a map so that I wouldn't get lost.

learn.def: result; starts a new sentence
learn.example: I was tired. That is why I went to bed.

learn.def: reason; followed by a noun, like 'because of'
learn.example: The flight was late due to fog.

sets.title: Comparing: like, as, similarly, unlike
sets.intro: Use 'like', 'as', 'the same as' and 'similar to' to show things are alike, and 'unlike' or 'different from' to show a difference. 'Similarly' and 'likewise' start a new sentence and are followed by a comma. Remember: 'as' is for a job or role (She works as a nurse), 'like' is for similarity (She looks like her mother).

learn.def: shows similarity; followed by a noun or pronoun
learn.example: She looks like her mother.

learn.def: for a job or role (as a teacher), or followed by a clause (as I said)
learn.example: He works as a driver.

learn.def: shows two things are equal
learn.example: This bag is as heavy as that one.

learn.def: shows two things are identical
learn.example: My phone is the same as yours.

learn.def: shows two things are almost the same
learn.example: Her house is similar to ours.

learn.def: shows two things are not the same (also: different to)
learn.example: My job is different from yours.

learn.def: shows a difference between two people or things
learn.example: Unlike me, he loves spicy food.

learn.def: starts a new sentence that is like the one before; comma after it
learn.example: Dogs need exercise. Similarly, cats need to play.

learn.def: starts a new sentence with the same idea; comma after it
learn.example: Anna is very kind. Likewise, her sister is helpful.

learn.def: shows the same method or idea; often followed by 'as' or a comma
learn.example: In the same way, you can learn to cook.

learn.def: puts two things side by side to see the difference
learn.example: Compared to my old car, this one is fast.

watch.wrong: She works like a teacher.
watch.right: She works as a teacher.
watch.why: Use 'as' for a real job or role; 'like' means 'similar to'.

watch.wrong: My phone is the same like yours.
watch.right: My phone is the same as yours.
watch.why: After 'the same' we use 'as', not 'like'.

watch.wrong: He is as tall than his father.
watch.right: He is as tall as his father.
watch.why: Use 'as ... as' for equal things, not 'than'.

sets.title: Result and degree: so/such ... that, too, enough
sets.intro: 'So ... that' and 'such ... that' show a result: 'so' goes before an adjective or adverb (so tired that), 'such' goes before a noun (such a long day that). 'Too' means more than we want (too hot), and 'enough' means as much as we need; it comes AFTER an adjective (big enough) and BEFORE a noun (enough money).

learn.def: so + adjective or adverb + that + result
learn.example: The soup was so hot that I couldn't eat it.

learn.def: such + (a/an) + (adjective) + noun + that + result
learn.example: It was such a hot day that we stayed inside.

learn.def: so much + uncountable noun + that
learn.example: There was so much noise that I couldn't sleep.

learn.def: so many + plural noun + that
learn.example: She has so many friends that she is never alone.

learn.def: too + adjective: more than is good or possible
learn.example: This bag is too heavy.

learn.def: too + adjective + to + verb: a negative result
learn.example: He is too tired to drive.

learn.def: too much + uncountable noun; too many + plural noun
learn.example: There are too many cars in the city.

learn.def: after an adjective (big enough) or before a noun (enough money)
learn.example: I don't have enough money.

learn.def: enough comes AFTER the adjective, then to + verb
learn.example: He is old enough to vote.

learn.def: less than we need
learn.example: There isn't enough milk for breakfast.

watch.wrong: It was such cold that we stayed home.
watch.right: It was so cold that we stayed home.
watch.why: Use 'so' before an adjective alone; use 'such' before a noun (such cold weather).

watch.wrong: She is enough old to drive.
watch.right: She is old enough to drive.
watch.why: 'Enough' goes after an adjective, not before it.

watch.wrong: I have too many work today.
watch.right: I have too much work today.
watch.why: 'Work' is uncountable, so use 'too much', not 'too many'.

sets.title: Contrast II: despite, whereas, nevertheless
sets.intro: 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or an -ing form, NOT a clause. Never say 'despite of'. 'Whereas' and 'while' compare two ideas. 'Nevertheless' and 'on the other hand' start a new sentence with a comma.

learn.def: followed by a noun or -ing; never 'despite of'
learn.example: Despite the rain, we went out.

learn.def: same as 'despite'; followed by a noun or -ing
learn.example: In spite of being tired, she worked.

learn.def: use it before a full clause (subject + verb)
learn.example: Despite the fact that he was ill, he worked.

learn.def: compares two facts; comma between the parts
learn.example: Ana likes coffee, whereas her sister likes tea.

learn.def: compares two facts; also means 'during the time that'
learn.example: While I prefer cities, he prefers villages.

learn.def: formal; starts a new sentence, comma after it
learn.example: The plan was risky. Nevertheless, they did it.

learn.def: starts a new sentence; comma after it
learn.example: It was cheap. Even so, I didn't buy it.

learn.def: gives a second, different point; comma after it; never 'in the other hand'
learn.example: Cars are fast. On the other hand, they are expensive.

learn.def: compares two things; comma after it
learn.example: Summers are hot. By contrast, winters are mild.

learn.def: says the opposite is true; not the same as 'on the other hand'
learn.example: He isn't lazy. On the contrary, he works very hard.

sets.title: Purpose and condition
sets.intro: Use 'in order to' and 'so as to' + a base verb to give a purpose. Use 'unless', 'as long as' and 'provided that' to set a condition. Remember: 'unless' already means 'if not', so do not add another negative.

learn.def: purpose; followed by the base verb
learn.example: She saved money in order to buy a car.

learn.def: purpose; followed by the base verb; not 'so as for'
learn.example: He left early so as to avoid the traffic.

learn.def: purpose; followed by a clause with can/could/would
learn.example: Speak slowly so that they can understand.

learn.def: means 'if not'; do not use another negative after it
learn.example: I won't go unless you come with me.

learn.def: condition; followed by a clause
learn.example: You can go out as long as you finish your homework.

learn.def: formal condition; followed by a clause
learn.example: I'll lend you money provided that you pay me back.

learn.def: same as 'provided that'; less formal
learn.example: Providing it doesn't rain, we'll have a picnic.

learn.def: formal; a strict condition
learn.example: He can stay on condition that he pays.

learn.def: starts a new sentence or follows a semicolon; comma after it
learn.example: Take a jacket. Otherwise, you'll be cold.

learn.def: followed by a clause; plan for a possible problem
learn.example: Take an umbrella in case it rains.

sets.title: Essay structure
sets.intro: A good essay uses connectors to guide the reader: one set for the first point, another to add points and one for the end. Most of these expressions start a sentence and are followed by a comma.

learn.def: opens the first point; comma after it
learn.example: Firstly, cars cause pollution.

learn.def: opens the first point; comma after it
learn.example: To begin with, the course is too long.

learn.def: opens the second point; comma after it
learn.example: Secondly, it is expensive.

learn.def: adds a strong extra point; formal; comma after it
learn.example: Moreover, the city has good transport.

learn.def: adds a strong extra point; formal; comma after it
learn.example: Furthermore, the job pays well.

learn.es: es más / lo que es más
learn.def: adds an even stronger point; comma after it
learn.example: What is more, it is free.

learn.def: starts the last paragraph; not 'in the conclusion'
learn.example: In conclusion, I agree with the idea.

learn.def: summarises the main points; comma after it
learn.example: To sum up, the plan has more benefits than risks.

learn.def: gives a general opinion after the details; comma after it
learn.example: On the whole, the trip was a success.

learn.def: gives a final general opinion; comma after it
learn.example: All in all, it was a good decision.

learn.def: similar to 'to sum up'; comma after it
learn.example: In summary, there are three main reasons.

sets.title: Emphasis and clarification
sets.intro: These connectors make a point stronger ('in fact', 'indeed'), restate it ('in other words', 'that is to say') or focus on the key idea ('above all', 'especially'). Most go at the start of a sentence with a comma; 'especially' and 'in particular' go next to the item they highlight. 'Indeed' and 'namely' sound more formal; 'actually' and 'as a matter of fact' are more spoken.

learn.def: adds a stronger or more exact point; comma after it
learn.example: I do not mind the rain. In fact, I like it.

learn.def: strengthens a point; formal
learn.example: The results were good; indeed, they were excellent.

learn.def: restates an idea in simpler words; comma after it
learn.example: The room is full. In other words, we cannot come in.

learn.def: explains exactly what you mean; usually between commas
learn.example: The test is optional, that is to say, nobody has to take it.

learn.def: introduces the most important point
learn.example: Above all, be honest with your clients.

learn.def: introduces the exact names or items you mean
learn.example: Two students won, namely Ana and Luis.

learn.def: puts the focus on one item of a group; often after it
learn.example: I like fruit, in particular mangoes.

learn.def: puts the focus on one item; goes before it; not 'specially'
learn.example: I love summer, especially the evenings.

learn.def: spoken; adds or corrects information
learn.example: As a matter of fact, I live next door.

learn.def: gives an exact detail; comma before or after it
learn.example: It was early, at 6:10 a.m. to be precise.

learn.def: adds a surprising fact or corrects an idea; NOT 'actualmente' (use 'currently')
learn.example: Actually, I come from Peru, not Spain.

sets.title: Time and sequence in narratives
sets.intro: These words order events in a story: 'meanwhile' (at the same time), 'eventually' and 'in the end' (the result), 'afterwards' (later) and 'from then on' (after that point). 'By the time', 'as soon as', 'until' and 'once' join clauses and take a present tense for the future. 'No sooner ... than' is formal and needs inversion ('No sooner had we left than ...').

learn.def: at the same time as another action; comma after it
learn.example: Anna cooked dinner. Meanwhile, Tom set the table.

learn.def: after a long time or many problems; NOT 'possibly'
learn.example: Eventually, the bus arrived.

learn.def: the final result after a process
learn.example: We argued for hours, but in the end we agreed.

learn.def: before or at a point; used with a present or past clause, not 'will'
learn.example: By the time we arrived, the film had started.

learn.def: immediately after something; present tense for the future
learn.example: I will call you as soon as I get home.

learn.def: one event right after another; inversion after 'no sooner'
learn.example: No sooner had we sat down than the lights went out.

learn.def: up to the moment something happens; no 'not' in the clause
learn.example: We waited until the rain stopped.

learn.def: later, after the event; comma after it
learn.example: We had lunch. Afterwards, we went for a walk.

learn.def: exactly at that point in the story
learn.example: At that moment, the phone rang.

learn.def: starting at that point and continuing

sets.title: Formal contrast and concession
sets.intro: In formal writing you can admit a point and still argue against it. 'Notwithstanding' works like 'despite' (+ noun). 'Albeit' means 'although it is' and is followed by an adjective or adverb. 'Be that as it may' is a fixed phrase.

learn.def: formal 'however'; comma after it
learn.example: The results were weak. Nonetheless, the team stayed optimistic.

learn.def: formal 'despite'; followed by a noun phrase, never 'of'
learn.example: Notwithstanding the delay, the event was a success.

learn.def: means 'although it is'; followed by an adjective or adverb
learn.example: She agreed, albeit reluctantly.

learn.def: a fixed phrase; admits a point, then moves on; comma after it
learn.example: Be that as it may, we must follow the rules.

learn.def: admits a point and adds a contrast; comma after it
learn.example: The data are limited. That said, the trend is clear.

learn.def: gives the opposite idea; comma after it
learn.example: Some benefit. Conversely, others lose out.

learn.def: contrast after a concession; comma after it at the start
learn.example: It is expensive. All the same, I want it.

learn.def: admits a point; followed by a comma and the argument
learn.example: Granted, the plan is risky, but it is worth trying.

learn.def: adds a balancing point; comma after it
learn.example: At the same time, we must reduce costs.

learn.def: contrast after a fact; comma after it
learn.example: He was ill. Even so, he went to work.

sets.title: Cause and effect in academic writing
sets.intro: Academic writing links causes and effects precisely. 'Owing to' and 'in view of' are followed by a noun phrase. 'Given that' and 'inasmuch as' are followed by a clause. 'Thereby' links an action to its result with an -ing form.

learn.def: result; starts a new sentence; comma after it
learn.example: The test failed. Consequently, the launch was delayed.

learn.def: result of an action; followed by an -ing form
learn.example: The firm cut waste, thereby saving money.

learn.def: formal result; often followed by a noun phrase
learn.example: The data are limited; hence the need for more research.

learn.def: formal result; can be followed by a clause or -ing
learn.example: Prices rose; thus, demand fell.

learn.def: formal result: 'in a way that fits the situation'
learn.example: Rules have changed; we must act accordingly.

learn.def: reason; followed by a noun phrase; never 'owing the'
learn.example: Owing to the strike, trains were cancelled.

learn.def: reason; followed by a clause
learn.example: Given that the budget is limited, we must choose carefully.

learn.def: reason; followed by a noun phrase
learn.example: In view of the risks, we should wait.

learn.def: reason; followed by a noun phrase
learn.example: As a consequence of the storm, flights stopped.

learn.def: very formal reason; followed by a clause
learn.example: The study is useful inasmuch as it shows a trend.

sets.title: Signposting and hedging
sets.intro: Signposting phrases guide the reader ('it is worth noting that', 'to put it another way'). Hedging words ('arguably', 'to some extent', 'broadly speaking') make a claim less absolute and more careful. Most of them start a sentence and take a comma.

learn.def: draws attention to a point; followed by a clause; 'worth noting', not 'worth to note'
learn.example: It is worth noting that the sample was small.

learn.def: restates an idea; comma after it
learn.example: To put it another way, the plan failed.

learn.def: restates or clarifies; commas around it
learn.example: The test is voluntary, that is to say, nobody must take it.

learn.es: es cierto que / hay que admitir
learn.def: admits a weak point before arguing; comma after it
learn.example: Admittedly, the results are weak.

learn.def: hedges a strong claim; goes before the word it softens
learn.example: This is arguably the best novel of the decade.

learn.def: a general statement with exceptions; comma after it
learn.example: Broadly speaking, the economy is improving.

learn.def: partly true; at the start or end
learn.example: To some extent, the criticism is fair.

learn.def: in most cases; comma after it
learn.example: By and large, the results are positive.

learn.def: introduces a topic; followed by a noun phrase
learn.example: With regard to costs, there is little to say.

learn.def: a careful way to report an idea; followed by a clause
learn.example: It would appear that the data are incomplete.

sets.title: Generalizing and exceptions
sets.intro: Use these phrases to make a general statement ('on the whole', 'as a rule', 'for the most part') or to exclude something ('apart from', 'with the exception of', 'other than', 'barring', 'save for'). General phrases usually start the sentence with a comma. 'With the exception of', 'barring' and 'save for' are formal; 'apart from' and 'other than' work in all registers. After 'apart from' and 'other than' use a noun or an -ing form.

learn.def: a general judgement, ignoring small details; comma after it
learn.example: On the whole, the conference was a success.

learn.def: usually, in most cases; at the start or before the verb
learn.example: As a rule, the shops close at eight.

learn.def: for most people or things; at the start or end
learn.example: In general, young people prefer apps to phone calls.

learn.def: mostly, with a few exceptions
learn.example: For the most part, the staff were helpful.

learn.def: mostly; formal
learn.example: In the main, the reforms have worked.

learn.def: excluding; also can mean 'in addition to'; + noun or -ing
learn.example: Apart from the price, the hotel was perfect.

learn.def: excluding one thing; formal; needs 'the'
learn.example: Everyone passed, with the exception of Pablo.

learn.def: excluding; often after 'nothing', 'anyone', 'anything'
learn.example: There was nothing to eat other than bread.

learn.def: unless something happens; + noun; formal
learn.example: Barring delays, we will arrive at noon.

learn.def: except; very formal; + noun
learn.example: The street was empty, save for a cat.

learn.def: in every case; at the end or start
learn.example: All the rules apply without exception.

sets.title: Reference and topic shift
sets.intro: These phrases introduce a topic ('regarding', 'with respect to', 'as regards', 'concerning'), move to another one ('as for', 'turning to'), go back ('returning to') or add a side comment ('incidentally', 'by the way'). 'As regards' and 'with reference to' are formal; 'as for', 'speaking of' and 'by the way' are more spoken. 'Regarding', 'concerning' and 'as for' are followed directly by a noun, never by 'to'.

learn.def: introduces a topic; formal; + noun phrase; no 'to'
learn.example: As regards the budget, we need more time.

learn.def: introduces a topic; formal; + noun phrase
learn.example: With respect to safety, the rules are clear.

learn.es: en cuanto a / en lo que respecta a
learn.def: moves to a new person or thing, often with a contrast; + noun
learn.example: As for Marta, she prefers to stay home.

learn.def: about; + noun; 'regarding to' is wrong
learn.example: I am writing regarding your letter of 5 May.

learn.def: about; formal; + noun
learn.example: There are new rules concerning noise.

learn.def: opens a letter or email about an earlier message
learn.example: With reference to your email, I attach the form.

learn.def: linked to an event or case; formal
learn.example: The police want to talk to him in connection with the theft.

learn.def: moves to the next topic; + noun; used in talks and reports
learn.example: Turning to costs, the figures are encouraging.

learn.def: reacts to a topic someone just mentioned; spoken
learn.example: Speaking of holidays, where are you going this year?

learn.def: adds a side comment; comma after it
learn.example: Incidentally, have you seen the new schedule?

learn.def: adds a side comment; spoken
learn.example: By the way, I met your brother yesterday.

learn.def: goes back to an earlier topic; + noun
learn.example: Returning to my first point, the cost is too high.

watch.why: 'As for' is followed directly by a noun; no 'to'.

sets.title: Advanced concession
sets.intro: Advanced writers show contrast in many ways. 'Much as', 'however much', 'no matter how' and the pattern 'adjective + as + subject + verb' ('Young as he is, ...', 'Strange as it may seem, ...') replace 'although' and sound formal. 'Granted', 'even so', 'for all that', 'that said' and 'all the same' come at the start of a new sentence, followed by a comma. Never add 'but' after 'much as' or 'however much'.

learn.def: 'although' for feelings or actions; start of sentence; no 'but' later
learn.example: Much as I admire her, I disagree with her plan.

learn.def: no matter how much; + subject + verb
learn.example: However much he tries, he cannot win.

learn.def: fixed pattern 'try as + subject + might'; formal
learn.example: Try as she might, she could not open the door.

learn.def: adjective + as + subject + verb; formal; inversion of 'although'
learn.example: Strange as it may seem, I enjoyed the exam.

learn.def: accepts a point, then argues against it; comma after it
learn.example: Granted, the plan is risky, but it could work.

learn.def: contrast with what was just said; comma after it
learn.example: The test was hard. Even so, most students passed.

learn.def: in spite of that; formal; at the start or end
learn.example: He is rude. For all that, people like him.

learn.def: adds a contrasting point; comma after it
learn.example: The food is good. That said, the service is slow.

learn.def: in spite of that; spoken or written
learn.example: It was raining. All the same, we went out.

learn.def: however; + adjective or adverb + subject + verb
learn.example: No matter how tired I am, I always cook dinner.

learn.def: whatever happens; formal; usually with 'will'
learn.example: Come what may, we will finish the project.

watch.wrong: Much as I like him, but I do not trust him.
watch.right: Much as I like him, I do not trust him.
watch.why: 'Much as' already contrasts: do not add 'but'.

watch.wrong: Strange as is it, I enjoyed the exam.
watch.right: Strange as it may seem, I enjoyed the exam.
watch.why: After 'adjective + as' use subject + verb: 'as it may seem'.

watch.wrong: However much he tries, he could not win.
watch.right: However much he tries, he cannot win.
watch.why: Keep the tenses consistent: present + present, or past + past.
